extracted.intended_audience: interest-group advocates and regulatory-affairs practitioners (and policy scholars)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for interest groups on designing and evaluating notice-and-comment submissions as part of a broader regulatory advocacy strategy, based on a 1992 vs. 2002 survey of tactics. Emphasizes combining formal comments with meetings, coordination, and record-building for multiple decision points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting formal comments during notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit formal written comments during the notice-and-comment process; this tactic was the most universally used and highly rated by surveyed organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat formal comments as the baseline tactic — they are widely used and considered highly effective. Ensure comments are timely and follow agency submission requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct contact with agency staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Engage in informal meetings or direct contact with agency rule writers and staff to influence rule development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use in-person or phone meetings to explain positions, clarify technical points, and build relationships; combine with written comments so staff have both formal record and interpersonal context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participating in agency-sponsored meetings or workshops
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend and participate in agency-run meetings, workshops, or hearings where the proposed rule is discussed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use workshops to raise issues, provide data, and signal engagement; reference workshop participation in subsequent written comments to show continuity of involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting comments at proposed and final rule stages with continuity of position
rubrics_metrics.description: File comments both at the proposed rule stage and again at the final rule stage, maintaining a consistent position across stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve continuity of arguments and phrasing so issues remain on the administrative record; repeat and refine prior points to ensure they're not lost between stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing comments at the ANPRM stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Submit comments during the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) stage as an early influence tactic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early engagement can shape the agency's initial approach; reference ANPRM comments later in the record to show precedence and sustained concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinating with other organizations to file aligned comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with allied organizations to submit coordinated or aligned comments to build a consistent record and amplify influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate messaging, data, and timing with coalitions or allies; consistent filings make it harder for agencies to ignore an issue and can be used to demonstrate broader stakeholder support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contacting the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) during regulatory review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reach out to OMB staff when the rule is undergoing OMB regulatory review as an additional leverage point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize OMB as another audience that can affect the rule; tailor messages to OMB concerns (costs, interagency impacts) and document contacts for the administrative record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engaging Congress to pressure the agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Use congressional engagement (briefings, letter campaigns, meetings with members/staff) to exert political pressure on agencies regarding a rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinate congressional outreach with comment submissions and other tactics; anticipate that congressional interest may change agency incentives or attract oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation as a last resort
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursue litigation only after administrative avenues (comments, meetings, OMB, Congress) have been exhausted or when preservation of record for court review is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use litigation strategically and expect it to be costly and adversarial; ensure earlier comments and record-building are phrased precisely to support potential judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference prior engagement in the comment
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the comment reflects and, where appropriate, cites prior meetings, ANPRM submissions, workshops, petitions, or related research by the commenter or allied organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly cite prior inputs to demonstrate sustained engagement and to connect the current comment to the existing administrative record; this helps preserve arguments across stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve multiple audiences with tone and content
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft comments with awareness that agency staff, OMB, Congress, and possibly courts will read them; tone and content should be appropriate for all these audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance technical detail for agency staff with higher-level policy/economic framing for OMB and political messaging for congressional audiences; avoid rhetoric that would undermine credibility in judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and preserve a record for multiple decision points
rubrics_metrics.description: Compose comments to preserve specific issues and precise phrasing for use at the proposed rule stage, final rule stage, and in potential litigation or oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, quotable language and document evidence and methodology so arguments can be relied upon later; treat comments as part of a durable paper trail rather than a one-off communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be part of a documented advocacy strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the comment is integrated into a documented organizational advocacy strategy (e.g., the organization is a known stakeholder, has position papers, and has met with staff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain records of outreach, position papers, and internal strategy so external filings can be linked to an organized campaign; agencies and courts give weight to documented, consistent advocacy.
